title: AI Inference Explained (2026): How Every AI Answer Is Made and Priced
summary: What AI inference is, how a prompt reaches a GPU (prefill, decode, KV cache, batching), why tokens get cheaper, and how teams can judge AI cost per task.
body_markdown:
Every time you ask an AI a question, a machine in a data center does a few billion multiplications to write your answer, one small piece of a word at a time. That work has a name: **inference** . It is the step you pay for every day, long after a model has finished training.


Most people meet inference only as a price on a pricing page ("$0.50 per million output tokens") or as a pause before a chatbot starts to type. Both come from the same physics. This guide follows one request from your prompt to a GPU and back, then explains why the price of that work keeps falling, who sells it, and what it means for a team that has to pick AI tools and pay for them.


> **TL;DR:** AI inference is the work a model does each time you use it: **prefill** reads your prompt, then **decode** writes the answer token by token. Cached input can cost 10 to 30 times less than fresh input, but cost per task decides your bill. Taskade runs no GPUs. Pro and up can bring their own key.[See the models →](https://www.taskade.com/models)


**Quick answer: what is AI inference?** AI inference is the step where a trained model answers new input. For a large language model, LLM inference runs in two phases: prefill reads the whole prompt at once, and decode writes the reply one token at a time while a KV cache keeps the work already done. Training happens once. Inference runs on every request, so it sets the speed and the cost of every AI tool.

## 🧠 What Is AI Inference?


**AI inference is the act of running a trained AI model on new input to produce an output.** For a language model, the input is your prompt and the output is text, written one[token](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/token) at a time. Every chatbot reply, every[AI agent](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-are-ai-agents) step and every AI automation is one or more inference calls, and each call is billed by the tokens it reads and writes.


A model has two lives. In training, engineers show it huge amounts of text and adjust its billions of weights until it predicts the next token well. That job runs once per model version and can take months. In inference, the finished model sits in GPU memory and answers requests, in seconds, all day. The[inference wiki entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/inference) covers the formal definition. The table below covers the practical one.


Training Inference


What it does Builds the model by adjusting its weights Uses the finished model to answer requests


How often it runs Once per model version Every prompt, every agent step, every day


What it optimizes Model quality Speed and cost per answer


Who pays The AI lab Every company and person that uses AI


Unit of cost GPU-months for one large job Price per million tokens, or per task


What you feel Nothing directly The wait before the first word, and the bill


The short version: **training decides how smart a model is, and inference decides how fast and how cheap each answer is.** Because inference repeats for every use, it is the cost that grows with your team's adoption. The[inference cost wiki entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/inference-cost) and our guide to[AI cost per task](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-cost-per-task) go deeper on the bill itself.

## 🏋️ Inference vs Training: How Do Compute, Cost and Hardware Differ?


**Inference vs training comes down to one big job against millions of small ones.** Training a model runs once on a huge cluster for weeks. Inference runs a forward pass for every token of every answer, for as long as the model is in use. A common rule of thumb from the 2020 OpenAI scaling-laws paper puts training at about 6 × N × D operations and inference at about 2 × N per token, where N is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens.


The rule makes the trade-off easy to compute. Take a dense 70-billion-parameter model trained on 15 trillion tokens:


```text
TRAINING VS INFERENCE COMPUTE  (rule of thumb, dense model) N = 70 billion parameters        D = 15 trillion training tokens
training  ≈ 6 × N × D  = 6 × 70e9 × 15e12   ≈ 6.3 × 10^24 operations, once  inference ≈ 2 × N      = 2 × 70e9           ≈ 1.4 × 10^11 operations per token
break-even = training ÷ inference per token  = 6.3e24 ÷ 1.4e11                ≈ 45 trillion tokens  (= 3 × D)
at   1 trillion tokens served per day  →  inference matches training in ~45 days  at 100 billion tokens served per day   →  ~450 days
For a mixture-of-experts model, use the ACTIVE parameters for the  per-token cost: Kimi K3 reads ~104B of its ~2.8T parameters per token.
```


The chart shows the same arithmetic over time. The flat line is the one-time training run. The bars are inference compute added up day by day at 1 trillion tokens a day.


Real fleets point the same way. Google researchers led by David Patterson reported in 2022 that inference used about three fifths of Google's machine learning energy, and training about two fifths, across sample weeks in 2019, 2020 and 2021. Reasoning models push the share further toward inference, because they spend extra[test-time compute](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/test-time-compute) on hidden tokens before they answer.

The[model training wiki entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/model-training) covers the training side, and the[scaling laws entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/scaling-laws) explains where the 6 × N × D rule comes from. The difference matters to a buyer for one reason: a lab pays for training once, but your team pays for inference on every use, through credits, a subscription or a provider bill.

## 🗺️ What Are the Types of AI Inference, and Where Does It Run?


**AI inference comes in three delivery types and runs in four kinds of place.** Real-time inference answers one request while a person waits. Streaming inference shows the answer as the model writes it. Batch inference processes many requests later, often at half the price. The place, from a cloud data center to a phone, sets the speed, the privacy and the bill.


Type How it works Typical use Price signal


Real-time (online) One request in, one answer out, while a person waits Chat, search, a live support agent The provider's list price per token


Streaming The answer arrives token by token while decode runs Chat apps that show words as they appear Same price as real-time, a faster feel


Batch You submit many requests and collect the results later Tagging a backlog, nightly reports, model evaluations About 50% off at OpenAI and Anthropic (checked 2026-10-19)


The batch discount is written into both labs' documentation. OpenAI's Batch API guide states a 50% discount against its synchronous API and a 24-hour completion window. Anthropic's Message Batches documentation states the same 50% and says most batches finish in less than an hour. A background job that nobody watches is the natural place to use it.

## 🛤️ How Does an AI Request Travel From Your Prompt to a GPU?


**An AI request passes through six stops: your app, a provider's API, a router, a queue, a GPU that runs prefill and decode, and a stream back to your screen.** The first word you see marks the end of prefill. Every word after it is one turn of the decode loop. Most of what you pay for happens inside the GPU stop.


Here is the whole journey in one diagram. Read it top to bottom.


```text
YOUR SCREEN
│  "Summarize this contract in five bullets"  (+ the contract, + app instructions)
▼
APP (for example, an AI workspace)
│  adds system instructions, picks a model, sends an API call
▼
PROVIDER API ──────────────► bills you per million tokens in and out
│
▼
ROUTER ── which copy of the model has room, and which one already
│      holds this prompt's start in its KV cache?
▼
QUEUE ── waits for a free slot in the next batch
│
▼
GPU NODE (weights already loaded in high-bandwidth memory)
│  1. TOKENIZE   text  ──►  token IDs
│  2. PREFILL    read every prompt token at once     (compute-bound)
│  3. KV CACHE   store keys and values for each token (memory)
│  4. DECODE     write 1 token, append, repeat        (memory-bound)
│       └─ loop runs once per output token
▼
STREAM ── tokens turn back into text and appear on screen
wait before the first word  = TTFT  (time to first token)
speed after the first word  = tokens per second


```


The same flow as a timed exchange shows where each wait comes from.


Two facts fall out of this picture. **A long prompt makes you wait longer before the first word** , because prefill must read all of it. **A long answer makes the request take longer and cost more** , because decode runs once per output token. That is why a pricing page lists input and output tokens separately.

## ⏱️ How Does LLM Inference Work? One Request, Token by Token


**LLM inference works as a short prefill followed by a long loop: the model reads the whole prompt once, then repeats one decode step per output token until it writes a stop token.** To make that concrete, this section follows one request with real timings. The numbers come from the Lambda benchmark cited below: an 8-GPU NVIDIA HGX B200 node with vLLM, 32 users at once, 8,192 input tokens per request, a mean 1,186 ms to the first token and 28.50 tokens per second per user.


The request: an operations lead pastes a contract and asks for five bullets. With the app's instructions and the contract, the prompt is **8,192 tokens** . The answer will be **400 tokens** . One decode step at 28.50 tokens per second takes about **35 milliseconds** .


Step What happens Clock time


1. Tokenize The text becomes 8,192 token IDs from the model's vocabulary A few milliseconds on a CPU


2. Route and queue The provider picks a model copy and waits for a slot in the next batch Part of the first-token wait


3. Prefill All 8,192 tokens pass through every layer in parallel. Keys and values for each token go into the KV cache Part of the first-token wait


4. First token The last position's output becomes a score for every vocabulary token, and the sampler picks one 1.19 s after send (TTFT)


5. Decode loop Each step feeds the newest token through every layer, reads the whole KV cache and the weights, and samples the next token About 35 ms per token


6. Stop The model writes its end token or reaches the output limit 15.2 s after send


7. Bill The provider reports 8,192 input and 400 output tokens After the stream ends


```text
ONE REQUEST, TOKEN BY TOKEN   (Lambda B200 benchmark rates, 32 users per node) t = 0.000 s   send 8,192-token prompt  t = 1.186 s   token   1  appears          ← TTFT: queue + prefill  t = 1.221 s   token   2                   ← every later token ≈ 35 ms apart  t = 1.502 s   token  10  t = 4.661 s   token 100  t = 8.171 s   token 200  t = 15.19 s   token 400  + end token      ← end-to-end latency
time spent before the first word   ≈  1.2 s   ( 8% of the request)  time spent writing the answer      ≈ 14.0 s   (92% of the request)
```


The split surprises most people. The prompt was 20 times longer than the answer, yet **92% of the clock time went to writing the answer** , because prefill handles thousands of tokens in one parallel pass and decode handles one token per pass. The cumulative clock looks like this:


### 🔬 What Happens Inside One Decode Step?


**One decode step pushes a single new token through every layer of the model, then turns the last layer's output into a probability for every token in the vocabulary.** In each layer, the attention part compares the new token with every earlier token through the KV cache, and the feed-forward part (or the chosen experts, in a mixture-of-experts model) transforms it. At the end, a sampler picks the next token, guided by settings such as[temperature](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/temperature) .


Three details explain behavior people notice. First, the model never "plans" the whole answer in one step: it commits to one token at a time, which is why[next-token prediction](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/next-token-prediction) is the right mental model. Second, the sampler is why the same prompt can give different answers: at a temperature above zero, it draws from the probabilities instead of always taking the top one. Third, a[tokenizer](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/tokenizer) splits text into sub-word pieces, so "tokens per second" is not "words per second": an English word averages about 1.3 tokens.

### 📏 The Five Numbers That Describe Inference Speed


**Inference speed is described by five numbers, and each one answers a different question.** The worked request above produces all five. Vendors quote different ones, so it pays to know which number a benchmark reports before you compare two hosts.


Metric Question it answers Value in the example


TTFT (time to first token) How long until the first word appears? 1.19 s


TPOT or ITL (time per output token, inter-token latency) How far apart are the words after that? About 35 ms


End-to-end latency How long until the answer is complete? 15.2 s for 400 tokens


Throughput How many tokens does the whole node write per second? 911.92 tokens per second


Goodput How much of that throughput meets the speed targets? Depends on the TTFT and TPOT targets you set


NVIDIA's inference glossary defines goodput as throughput measured while the system keeps its TTFT and TPOT targets. A provider can always raise raw throughput by packing more users into a batch, so goodput counts only the tokens that arrived fast enough to be useful.

## ⚡ What Are Prefill and Decode?


**Prefill and decode are the two phases of every AI answer.** Prefill reads the whole prompt in one parallel pass and is limited by compute. Decode writes the answer one token at a time and is limited by[memory bandwidth](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/infrastructure/memory-bandwidth) , because each new token needs another read of the model's weights. The pause before the first word is prefill. The steady typing after it is decode.


An analogy helps. Prefill is a reader who scans a whole page at once. Decode is a writer who must reopen a heavy reference book before every single word. The writer is slow, not because thinking is hard, but because fetching the book takes time. On a[GPU](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/infrastructure/gpu) , "the book" is tens or hundreds of gigabytes of weights in high-bandwidth memory.


Prefill Decode


What it does Reads every prompt token at once Writes one output token per step


Bottleneck Compute (math units) Memory bandwidth (moving weights)


What you feel The wait before the first word (TTFT) The writing speed after it


Grows with Prompt length Answer length


Price signal Input tokens, usually cheaper Output tokens, usually several times more


A real benchmark shows both numbers at once. Lambda ran DeepSeek-V4-Pro with vLLM on one NVIDIA HGX B200 node (8 GPUs), with 32 requests in parallel, 8,192 input tokens and 2,048 output tokens each. It measured **911.92 output tokens per second** in total, **28.50 tokens per second per user** , and a mean wait of **1,186 milliseconds** before the first token. The same node writes about 32 times faster in total than it does for any one person, because it serves 32 people at once.


That gap between per-user speed and per-server speed is the whole economics of inference in one line. A person feels the per-user number. The provider pays rent with the per-server number. Our[tokens per second wiki entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/tokens-per-second) explains both measures and how vendors quote them.


> **Citation capsule:** In Lambda's benchmark of DeepSeek-V4-Pro on one 8-GPU NVIDIA HGX B200 node with vLLM, 32 parallel requests produced 911.92 output tokens per second in total but 28.50 tokens per second for each user, with a 1.19-second mean time to first token. Per-server throughput pays for the hardware, and per-user speed is what a reader sees.


### 🧮 Why Is Decode Memory-Bound? The Back-of-Envelope Math


**Decode is memory-bound because every new token requires reading every active weight from GPU memory, and a GPU can do math far faster than it can move those bytes.** A one-line formula gives the ceiling on per-user speed for a single user with nobody else in the batch: memory bandwidth divided by the bytes read per token.


```text
DECODE SPEED CEILING, ONE USER ALONE ON THE GPU max tokens per second  ≈  memory bandwidth  ÷  bytes of weights read per token
70B dense model in FP8 (1 byte per weight)  →  ~70 GB read per token
1 × H100   3.35 TB/s  ÷ 70 GB  ≈   48 tokens per second, at best  1 × B300   8.0  TB/s  ÷ 70 GB  ≈  114 tokens per second, at best
the same model in FP4 (0.5 byte per weight)  →  ~35 GB per token  1 × B300   8.0  TB/s  ÷ 35 GB  ≈  228 tokens per second, at best
Real speeds land below the ceiling: the KV cache is read too,  and kernels never reach 100% of peak bandwidth.
```


The same formula explains why batching is so cheap. With 32 users in a batch, the GPU still reads the 70 GB of weights **once per step** , but it writes 32 tokens instead of 1. The math units, which sat idle while bytes arrived, finally have work to do. Engineers call this raising the arithmetic intensity: more operations for each byte moved. It is also why[HBM](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/infrastructure/hbm) , the stacked memory beside each GPU, matters more for inference than raw compute does.

### 🏎️ How Hosts Raise Per-User Speed: Speculative Decoding


**Speculative decoding raises per-user speed by letting a small draft model guess several tokens ahead, which the large model then checks in a single pass.** Decode is slow because every token needs another read of the weights and the cache from memory. If the large model accepts four guessed tokens in one step, the reader gets four tokens for about the price of one memory read. The answer does not change, because the large model throws away any guess it would not have written itself.


Speculator method Paper How the draft works


EAGLE-3 arXiv 2503.01840 (2025) A light draft layer predicts the next tokens from the target model's own hidden states


DFlash arXiv 2602.06036 (2026) A block-diffusion drafter proposes a whole block of tokens at once


DSpark arXiv 2607.05147 (2026) A semi-autoregressive drafter schedules its guesses by how confident it is


All three methods train the draft on the target model's hidden states. That means a host builds its best speculator after the model is already serving real traffic, which is one reason a host's speed on a new model can keep rising after launch day. Baseten lists all three as speculator options in its[day-zero write-up on Kimi K3](https://www.baseten.co/blog/how-to-build-a-day-zero-api-for-kimi-k3/) .


**Same weights, different speed.** On 2026-10-20,[Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/kimi-k3/providers) listed median output speeds for Kimi K3 on selected hosts. LithosAI's Ultra Chat endpoint led at about 422 tokens per second. Nebius ran about 192, Amazon Bedrock about 142, Fireworks about 112, Baseten about 96, Together AI about 57, and Moonshot's own API about 42. That is a ten-times spread between the fastest host and the lab itself, for identical weights. The chips, the parallelism, the batch sizes and the speculators make the difference. ## 🗄️ What Is the KV Cache, and Why Does Caching Cut the Bill?


**The KV cache is the stored result of the work a model has already done on the tokens it has read.** It keeps the attention "keys" and "values" for each token in GPU memory, so the model does not recompute them for every new word. When a new request starts with exactly the same text as an earlier one, a provider can reuse that cache and charge the repeated input tokens at a deep discount.


Without a KV cache, the model would reread your entire prompt before every word it writes. With it, the model reads the prompt once, then each decode step adds one entry. The[KV cache wiki entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/kv-cache) shows the mechanics. What matters for cost is the second trick, **prompt caching** : keeping the cache after a request ends, labeled by the exact text that produced it.


AI tools resend the same opening text constantly. A chat app resends the whole thread on every turn. An agent resends its instructions and tool list on every step. A team assistant opens every conversation with the same company instructions. If the start of the prompt matches, the provider skips most of the prefill. The provider's side of the same story is just as large. In its Open Source Week write-up, DeepSeek reported that over one 24-hour window, 342 billion of its 608 billion input tokens, or **56.3%** , hit its on-disk KV cache. More than half of the reading work was already done before the request arrived.


One rule makes or breaks caching: **the match is exact, from the first token.** Change one word at the very start of a prompt, such as a timestamp in the instructions, and everything after it becomes fresh input again. Good AI tools keep the stable part of a prompt first and the changing part last. Our guides to[prompt caching](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/prompt-caching) and[how to reduce LLM costs](https://www.taskade.com/blog/reduce-llm-costs) show how to structure prompts so that the cache hits.


### 📐 KV Cache Explained in Numbers: How Big Does It Get?


**A KV cache grows by a fixed number of bytes for every token in the conversation, so its size is a simple product.** For a standard transformer, multiply 2 (one key and one value) by the number of layers, the number of key-value heads, the size of each head and the bytes per number. Then multiply by the tokens in the conversation and by the users in the batch.


Meta's Llama 3 70B is a good worked case, because its configuration is public: 80 layers, 64 query heads but only 8 key-value heads (a design called grouped-query attention, or GQA), and a head size of 128.


```text
KV CACHE SIZE  =  2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes per value × tokens Llama 3 70B, 16-bit cache:  2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes   =  327,680 bytes  ≈ 320 KiB per token
one   8,192-token chat        ≈  2.5 GiB  one 128,000-token document    ≈ 40   GiB   (half of one H100's memory)
How many 8,192-token chats fit beside the weights on 8 × H100 (640 GB)?  640 GB − ~70 GB of FP8 weights  ≈ 570 GB free  570 GB ÷ 320 KiB per token      ≈ 1.7 million tokens of cache  1.7 million ÷ 8,192             ≈ 210 chats at the same moment
```


That last line is the real limit on batch size, and therefore on price. Each design trick that shrinks the per-token cache lets one node serve more people at once. Grouped-query attention cut Llama 3 70B's cache eight times, compared with giving every one of its 64 query heads its own keys and values. Multi-head latent attention (MLA), which DeepSeek introduced and Kimi K3 uses on 24 of its layers, stores one compressed vector per token instead.


The full multi-head figure is a what-if for the same 70B shape with 64 key-value heads. The Kimi K3 figure covers only its 24 MLA layers. Its other 69 layers keep a fixed state instead, which the next section explains. The[context window wiki entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/context-window) and our[history of the context window](https://www.taskade.com/blog/context-window-history) show why longer contexts made this arithmetic the center of serving design.


### 🧮 Hybrid Models Keep Two Caches


**A hybrid model such as Kimi K3 keeps two kinds of cache, because it mixes two kinds of attention layer.** Of its 93 layers, 24 are Gated MLA (multi-head latent attention) layers, full attention that keeps a compact per-token cache like the one above. The other 69 are Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers, a form of linear attention that keeps one fixed-size state per conversation, however long the conversation grows. The stack repeats three KDA layers, then one MLA layer.


24 Gated MLA layers 69 KDA layers


Kind of attention Full attention over every earlier token Linear attention with a fixed-size memory


What it stores A small latent entry for every token One running state per conversation


Grows with context Yes, in a straight line No, same size at 10 tokens or 1M


Prefix reuse Exact, to the token From the nearest saved checkpoint


```text
KIMI K3: CACHE MEMORY FOR ONE CONVERSATION 24 MLA layers  ── per-token cache ── 576 values per layer per token  ≈ 13.5 KiB per token in FP8  ≈ 13.5 GiB at the full 1,048,576-token context
69 KDA layers  ── fixed state ────── ≈ 217 MB in BF16 for the whole model  ≈ 27 MB per GPU when split 8 ways (TP8)  the same at token 10 and at token 1,000,000
```


The two caches change how prompt caching works. An MLA cache can resume at the exact token where two prompts stop matching. A KDA state is a running summary, so it cannot be cut at an arbitrary token. The engine saves copies of the state at checkpoints, and a cached prefix resumes from the nearest checkpoint before the mismatch, then rereads the gap. Caching still skips most of the prefill, but it is coarser than on a pure-attention model, and the serving engine runs two memory allocators side by side, one for each kind of cache.


KDA is the latest step in a short line of linear attention research. Katharopoulos and colleagues in 2020 swapped softmax for a simple feature map, so each attention head keeps one fixed d × d state. DeltaNet added the delta rule, which edits the value stored under a key instead of only adding to it. Yang and colleagues made that rule train in parallel (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2406.06484). Gated DeltaNet added a forget gate (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2412.06464). KDA (arXiv 2510.26692, October 2025) lets each channel of the state forget at its own rate. The payoff is a cache that stays small at a million tokens, which is why Moonshot uses it for most of the stack.

## 📦 What Is Batching, and Why Does It Make Tokens Cheap?


**Batching means one GPU serves many requests in the same decode step.** Each step reads the model's weights from memory once, and that one read can produce a token for one user or for dozens. Because the memory read is the slow part, adding users to a batch costs little until the GPU runs out of memory or compute. Batching is the main reason a token costs fractions of a cent.


Early servers used static batches: a group of requests started together and the GPU waited until the longest one finished. In July 2022 the Orca paper at OSDI introduced iteration-level scheduling. Requests join and leave the batch at every single step, so a finished answer frees its slot at once. That idea, now called **continuous batching** , is standard in open-source servers such as vLLM. In September 2023, the PagedAttention paper behind vLLM added a second gain: it stores each request's KV cache in small fixed pages, the way an operating system pages memory, and reported **2 to 4 times higher throughput** than earlier systems at the same latency.


The limit is memory. Every user in the batch needs their own KV cache in GPU memory for the life of their request. The model weights take their share first, and only what is left holds caches. When it fills, new requests wait in the queue. That is why newer chips often add memory and bandwidth rather than raw math.


Batching also explains why scale matters so much to a provider. Here is an illustration with round numbers, not any company's real costs. Assume an 8-GPU node rents for **$6 per GPU-hour ($48 per hour)** and the provider earns **$7 for every million output tokens it serves** , counting the input tokens that come with them. Revenue per hour then depends only on throughput:


At the 912 tokens per second of the Lambda benchmark above, this node would earn about $23 an hour against $48 of rent. It breaks even only near **1,900 tokens per second of steady demand** , roughly twice that output, every hour of the day. The gap closes through bigger batches, more cache hits, faster kernels and fewer idle hours. That is the margin game every inference provider plays, and it is why the[companion deep dive](https://www.taskade.com/blog/inference-as-a-service) spends a full section on it.

## 🔀 What Does Routing Mean in AI Inference?


**Routing in AI inference means choosing where a request goes, and the word covers three different choices.** A model router picks which model answers. A provider router picks which company serves a given model. A replica router picks which copy of one model, on which GPU server, handles the request. Each choice changes speed, price and cache hits, so it helps to keep them apart.


The replica level is where caching meets routing. A plain load balancer spreads requests evenly across servers. For AI, that wastes work: your second message can land on a server that never saw your first, so the whole conversation is prefilled again from scratch. A cache-aware router sends you back to the server that already holds your prompt's start in its KV cache, unless that server is full. The open-source llm-d project, launched by Red Hat with CoreWeave, Google Cloud, IBM Research and NVIDIA in May 2025, does this on Kubernetes. Its site cites its own benchmarks of up to **3 times higher output throughput** and **2 times faster time to first token** .


A non-technical team only ever touches the top level. When an AI tool offers an **Auto** model setting, it is a model router: it decides which model fits each task so you do not have to read benchmark tables. The other two levels sit with the tool and its providers. They still show up in your experience as speed and as the price the tool can afford to charge.

### 🔄 What Happens to a Request Inside a Serving Engine?


**A serving engine such as vLLM moves each request through a short life: it waits in a queue, gets scheduled into a batch, prefills, decodes, and ends in one of three ways.** The scheduler re-plans the batch at every step. If GPU memory for the cache runs out, the engine can pause a running request, free its cache and put it back in the queue, a step called preemption.

### 🧱 Total Parameters, Not Active Ones, Set the GPU Bill


**A mixture-of-experts model saves memory traffic on each token, but it does not save GPU memory: the total parameter count, not the active count, decides how many GPUs a host must rent.** Kimi K3 has about 2.8 trillion parameters and uses about 104 billion of them, roughly 3.7%, on each token. Each token picks 16 of 896 routed experts plus 2 shared experts. A host still keeps all 896 experts loaded.


Batching is the reason. One user's token touches only 16 experts, but a production batch holds tokens from many users at once, and across that batch nearly every expert is busy at some point. Swapping experts in and out of GPU memory on demand would add a slow read to a decode step that should take milliseconds, and the host would miss the latency it promises. So the rule of thumb is: **active parameters set the speed per token, total parameters set the hardware bill.**

## 💸 Does a Cheaper Token Mean a Cheaper AI Bill?


**A cheaper token does not guarantee a cheaper bill, because the bill is cost per task, not cost per token.** Cost per task is the price per token multiplied by the tokens one job uses, plus retries and failed attempts. Reasoning models and AI agents can spend many more tokens on one job, so the price per token falls while the cost per finished task can rise.


Three numbers move in different directions at once:


1. **Sticker price per token has fallen** on most tiers since 2023, as the chart above shows.
2. **Price per unit of intelligence has collapsed.** Epoch AI's 9 to 900 times per year is the cost of holding a fixed benchmark score.
3. **Tokens per task have grown.** A reasoning model thinks in hidden tokens before it answers, and an agent runs many steps, each with its own prompt.


```text
COST PER TASK  =  [ (input tokens × input price)
+ (cached tokens × cached price)
+ (output tokens × output price, including hidden reasoning) ]
×  (attempts until the task is done)  Example shape for one agent job:  10 steps × 20,000 input tokens   = 200,000 input   (most of it cacheable)  10 steps ×  1,000 output tokens  =  10,000 output  1 retry                          =  ×2 if nothing is cached
```


This is why the[AI cost per task guide](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-cost-per-task) recommends a 20-task test on your own work before you compare tools, and why our[TSK benchmark](https://www.taskade.com/tsk) scores models on real builds instead of on price lists. A model that finishes a job in one try at a higher token price often beats a cheaper model that needs three tries.

### ✂️ How Do Hosts Split One Model Across Eight GPUs?


**Hosts split a giant model across GPUs in two main ways: tensor parallelism slices every layer, and expert parallelism places whole experts on specific GPUs.** The choice trades one user's latency against the total tokens a node serves.


TP8 (tensor parallelism) TP + EP (tensor plus expert parallelism)


Attention layers Sliced across all 8 GPUs Sliced across all 8 GPUs


Experts Every expert sliced across all 8 GPUs Whole experts placed on specific GPUs


Best at The lowest latency for one user More tokens per second per node


Main cost The most traffic between GPUs, after every layer A popular expert can overload the GPU that holds it


In plain words, TP8 is eight people each reading one eighth of every page, then comparing notes after every page. It is fast for one reader, but the note-passing never stops. TP + EP keeps that split for attention, then hands each person their own chapters of the expert library, so a token visits only the GPUs that hold the experts it picked.


TP + EP brings a new problem: hot experts. If many tokens in a batch pick experts that live on one GPU, that GPU sets the pace and the other seven wait. **Expert load balancing** watches which experts are busy and adds or removes extra copies of hot experts at run time, in the spare memory of the other GPUs.


Large hosts also split prefill and decode into separate pools of workers, the design Moonshot's own Mooncake paper described in 2024. Agent and long-context traffic sends long prompts and short answers, so hosts tend to add prefill capacity for it. ## 🏷️ Why Is the Lab's Own API Often the Cheapest?


**A lab's own API is often the cheapest place to run its model because the lab tunes its serving before the model ships.** It knows the model's exact shapes and precision, writes its GPU code in advance, and runs at a scale that keeps batches full. A third-party host must learn those details after the weights are public, then compete with the lab's price and with every other host.


DeepSeek is the clearest case on the public record. In its Open Source Week write-up, it reported that each H800 GPU node averaged about **73,700 input tokens per second** in prefill (cache hits included) and **14,800 output tokens per second** in decode. It also computed a theoretical cost-profit margin of **545%** , but only "if all tokens were billed" at its reasoning-model price, on an assumed $2 per H800 GPU-hour. DeepSeek itself said actual revenue was substantially lower, because of cheaper models, free services and night-time discounts. Treat the 545% as a ceiling for an ideal week, not a profit report.


Third parties still win business on first-party models. They win on **consistency** : a lab that cannot buy enough GPUs for its own demand can slow down or pause signups, while a host with spare capacity keeps serving. They win on **speed** , where custom chips lead. And they win on **contracts** : a company that already buys from one cloud often prefers to keep AI spending on the same bill.

**AI inference in 2026 changes in six ways: hybrid attention shrinks the cache, native 4-bit weights shrink the model, speculators arrive after launch, prefill and decode move to separate fleets, routers follow the cache, and agents multiply the tokens per task.** Each shift moves cost or speed by a large factor, and most of them come from the model's design, not only from new chips.


Shift What changed Where you see it


Hybrid attention Most layers use linear attention with a fixed-size state, a few keep full attention Kimi K3: 69 KDA layers and 24 MLA layers, a 1,048,576-token context


Native low precision Models train with 4-bit weights instead of being shrunk after training OpenAI's gpt-oss (August 2025) and Kimi K3 ship MXFP4 weights


Speculators after launch Hosts train a draft model on the target model's hidden states once it serves traffic EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark, and host speeds that rise after day zero


Disaggregated serving Prefill and decode run on separate pools of GPUs, sized per workload Mooncake, DistServe, NVIDIA Dynamo, and the 2026 "Prefill-as-a-Service" proposal


Cache-aware routing Routers send a request to the replica that already holds its prefix llm-d on Kubernetes, and cheaper cached input on most price lists


More tokens per task Reasoning models and multi-step agents read and write far more per job Cost per task rising on some jobs while the price per token falls


The first two shifts attack memory: ahybrid cache stays a fixed size on most layers, and 4-bit weights halve the bytes read per decode step. The third, covered in thespeculative decoding section , is why a model can get faster on one host months after release.

## 📖 AI Inference Glossary: Terms in Plain English


**These definitions stand alone, so each one can be read without the rest of this guide.** They use the words that appear on pricing pages, in benchmarks and in AI tool settings.


Term Plain-English definition


Inference Running a trained AI model on new input to produce an answer


Token A small piece of text, about three quarters of an English word, that models read and write


Prompt Everything sent to the model: your message, instructions, files and chat history


Prefill The first phase of an answer, when the model reads the whole prompt at once


Decode The second phase, when the model writes the answer one token at a time


KV cache Stored keys and values for tokens already read, so the model does not redo that work


Prompt caching Keeping the KV cache after a request so that a repeated prompt start is billed at a discount


TTFT Time to first token: the wait before the first word appears


Tokens per second Writing speed, quoted per user or for a whole server


P95 latency The wait that 95 of every 100 requests beat, a fairer speed number than the average


Batch inference Sending many requests at once for results later, usually at a discount


Edge inference Running a model close to the data, on a local server or device, instead of in a distant cloud


NPU A small AI unit built into a phone or laptop chip for on-device inference


Batching Serving many requests in the same model step to share each memory read


Continuous batching Letting requests join and leave a batch at every step instead of waiting for the slowest


Memory bandwidth How fast a chip moves data from memory to its math units, the limit on decode speed


Mixture of experts A model design that reads only part of its weights for each token


Open-weight model A model whose trained weights are public, so any provider can serve it


Frontier model A leading model from a top AI lab, usually served only by that lab or its partners


Inference provider A company that runs models on its hardware and sells access by the token


Router Software that picks a model, a provider or a GPU server for each request


BYOK Bring your own key: a tool sends requests to a provider on your own account


Cost per task What one finished job costs, including every step and retry


TPOT / ITL Time per output token, or inter-token latency: the gap between words after the first one


Goodput Throughput counted only while answers still meet their speed targets


Quantization Storing weights or cache entries in fewer bits, for example FP8 or FP4, to move fewer bytes


Speculative decoding A draft model guesses several tokens and the main model checks them in one pass


GQA Grouped-query attention: several query heads share one set of keys and values, so the cache shrinks


MLA Multi-head latent attention: the cache stores one compressed vector per token


Linear attention Attention that keeps a fixed-size state instead of a per-token cache


Chunked prefill Splitting a long prompt into pieces so other users keep getting tokens


Disaggregated serving Running prefill and decode on separate pools of GPUs


Serving engine The software that loads the weights and runs batching and caching, for example vLLM

## 💬 Frequently Asked Questions About AI Inference


What is AI inference?


AI inference is the work a trained AI model does each time you use it. The model reads your prompt as tokens, runs them through its network on a GPU or another accelerator, and writes the answer one token at a time. Training builds the model once. Inference runs it again for every question, agent step and automation, so it is the recurring cost of any AI product.


What are the types of AI inference?


AI inference comes in three delivery types. Real-time inference answers one request while a person waits. Streaming inference shows the answer token by token as it is written. Batch inference processes many requests later, and OpenAI and Anthropic both list a 50% discount for batch jobs. Inference also runs in four kinds of place: the cloud, on-premise servers, edge servers and on-device chips.


What is the difference between AI training and inference?


Training is a large, slow job that adjusts a model's weights by showing it huge amounts of data, and it runs once per model version. Inference is the use of the finished model: it answers requests in seconds, millions of times a day. Training decides how smart a model is. Inference decides how fast and how cheap each answer is.


What are prefill and decode in AI inference?


Prefill and decode are the two phases of every AI answer. In prefill, the model reads the whole prompt at once in parallel, which is limited by compute and causes the pause before the first word. In decode, the model writes one token at a time, and each step reads the weights from memory, so decode is limited by memory bandwidth.


What is a KV cache?


A KV cache is the stored work a model has already done on the tokens it has read. It holds the attention keys and values for each token, so the model does not redo that work for every new word. When a new request starts with the same text as an earlier one, a provider can reuse the cache and bill those input tokens at a large discount.


Why do output tokens cost more than input tokens?


Output tokens cost more because the model writes them one at a time, and each one needs a full pass over the weights in memory. Input tokens are read in one parallel burst. On October 18, 2026, OpenAI listed GPT-6 Luna at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, a five-times gap.


Why are AI tokens getting cheaper?


Tokens get cheaper because serving software improves, chips gain memory bandwidth, models become more efficient, and many providers compete to serve the same open-weight models. Epoch AI measured in March 2025 that the price to reach a fixed level of performance fell between 9 and 900 times per year, depending on the task.


Does a cheaper price per token mean a cheaper AI bill?


Not always. The bill depends on cost per task: the price per token multiplied by the tokens a task uses, plus retries. Reasoning models and agents can use many more tokens for one job, so a cheaper token can still produce a bigger bill. Measure one finished task on your own work before you compare tools.


What is the difference between open-weight and frontier models?


An open-weight model publishes its weights, so any provider can serve it and many companies compete on its price. A frontier model is usually closed and served by its lab or the lab's partners. Menlo Ventures reported in December 2025 that open-source models held 11% of enterprise LLM usage, down from 19% a year earlier.


What does tokens per second measure?


Tokens per second measures how fast a model writes. Per-user tokens per second is the speed one person sees. Per-server tokens per second is the total output across everyone a server handles at once, which pays for the hardware. A good AI tool needs a short wait before the first word and a steady speed after it.


Why can't Kimi K3 run on one GPU?


Kimi K3 has about 2.8 trillion parameters, and its MXFP4 checkpoint is about 1.56 TB. One NVIDIA B300 GPU holds 288 GB, so the weights alone fill more than five of them, and hosts serve each copy on one eight-GPU node, about 2.3 TB, which leaves room for the cache. Eight B200 GPUs hold only 1.44 TB, and eight H100 GPUs hold 640 GB. Only about 104 billion parameters work on each token, but across a production batch every expert is busy at some moment, so all of them must stay in GPU memory.


Why does the same model run at different speeds on different providers?


Each host serves the same weights with its own chips, parallelism, batch sizes, caching and speculative decoding. On October 20, 2026, Artificial Analysis listed Kimi K3 at about 422 tokens per second on the fastest host and about 42 on Moonshot's own API, a ten-times spread for one model. A tool that buys tokens from a host inherits that host's speed.


What does BYOK mean in AI tools?


BYOK means bring your own key. You add an API key from an AI provider to a tool, and the tool sends requests to that provider on your account, so the provider bills you directly. In Taskade, Pro and up can add OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Vertex AI keys for custom agents, Ask Agent and automation AI steps, and Business and up can add more providers. Taskade EVE builds and edits can run on those keys too when you pick a model under **Your keys** . Each Taskade EVE step or automation AI step on your key uses a fixed step fee in credits, and each agent step uses it after your plan's included monthly key steps.


What is LLM inference?


LLM inference is the process of running a trained large language model to generate text from a prompt. The model splits the prompt into tokens, reads them in one prefill pass that fills a KV cache, then writes the answer one token at a time in a decode loop. Each output token needs another read of the weights from GPU memory, which is why long answers take longer and cost more.


How does LLM inference work step by step?


A request is tokenized, routed to a copy of the model and queued for the next batch. Prefill reads every prompt token and fills the KV cache. The model then samples the first token, streams it, and repeats the decode step until it writes a stop token. In Lambda's benchmark of an 8,192-token prompt on an 8-GPU B200 node, the first token came after about 1.2 seconds and later tokens about 35 milliseconds apart.


How much does AI inference cost?


AI inference is priced per million tokens, with output several times dearer than input. On October 18, 2026, OpenAI listed GPT-6 Luna at $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million tokens, and GPT-6.1 Sol at $2 and $10. A ten-step agent job that reads 200,000 tokens and writes 10,000 costs about 50 cents on GPT-6.1 Sol with no caching, and about 16 cents when 90% of the input is cached.


Is inference more expensive than training?


One answer costs far less than training, but inference repeats for every request, so over a model's life it often costs more. A rule of thumb puts training at about 6 × parameters × training tokens and inference at about 2 × parameters per token. By that rule, a model matches its training compute after serving about three times as many tokens as it trained on. Google reported that inference used about three fifths of its machine learning energy in 2019 to 2021.


How big is a KV cache?


A KV cache stores a key and a value per layer, per key-value head, per head dimension, for every token. Llama 3 70B has 80 layers, 8 key-value heads and a head size of 128, so a 16-bit cache needs about 320 KiB per token, or about 40 GiB for one 128,000-token conversation. Kimi K3 needs about 13.5 KiB per token on its 24 MLA layers, plus a fixed state on its 69 linear attention layers.


What is speculative decoding?


Speculative decoding writes several tokens per decode step. A small draft model guesses the next few tokens, and the large model checks all of them in one pass, keeping only the ones it would have written itself. The answer stays the same, but each memory read of the large model can produce several tokens. EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark are recent speculator methods.


Does Taskade run its own GPUs?


No. Taskade runs no GPUs of its own. It sends each AI request to a model provider that runs frontier models from top AI labs, and it focuses on the workspace around the model: projects, AI agents, automations and Taskade Genesis apps. Auto is the default model setting, and Claude runs on your own API key in custom agents on Pro and up.
